title: How Consonants Work: Stops and Air
label: Lesson 02

goal.html: Today's goal: Control where and how the air stops in /p b t d k ɡ/ — especially the puff after /p t k/, the missing puff after /s/, and final stops with no 으.
By the end, spin sounds like s+삔 (not 스핀), and bed stays one beat (not 베-드).

blocks.html: Marks: ● strong beat · · weak beat · CAPITALS = stressed · | = small pause · ‿ = link. Full key in Lesson 01.
01 / Understand the pattern
1. Three questions for every consonant
Where does the air stop? (lips, tongue tip, back of tongue)
How does it move? (a full stop, a hiss, through the nose...)
Is your voice on? Put your fingers on your throat and say sss → zzz. The buzz you feel on /z/ is voicing.
Today's six sounds are stops: the air is blocked completely for a moment, and then released.

rows.html: Press your lips together, then pop them open.
The tongue tip touches the ridge behind the top teeth, not the teeth themselves.
The back of the tongue rises and touches the soft palate.

blocks.html: The letter g is not always /ɡ/: go has /ɡ/, but giant has /dʒ/.

blocks.alt: Where the air stops: both lips /p b/, tongue tip /t d/, back of tongue /k ɡ/. Top: side view. Bottom: front view.

blocks.text: 2. English has two stops where Korean has three
blocks.html: 2. English has two stops where Korean has three
Korean has three kinds of stops at each place (ㅂ/ㅃ/ㅍ, ㄷ/ㄸ/ㅌ, ㄱ/ㄲ/ㅋ). English has only two (/p/–/b/). The good news: your Korean sounds are a useful starting point.

rows.html: /p t k/ at the start of a stressed syllable
A strong puff of air, just like ㅍ ㅌ ㅋ. Hold a tissue in front of your mouth: it should move.
Little or no puff. Start your voice early, as if you hum a tiny "m" first: (m)bag. Never use ㅃ ㄸ ㄲ.
No puff. spin ≈ s+삔, stop ≈ s+땁, sky ≈ s+까이. Korean spelling (스핀, 스톱, 스카이) adds a puff and an extra 으 beat.

blocks.text: 3. Stops at the end of a word
blocks.html: 3. Stops at the end of a word
The s+ㄲ trick: Say 까이 (tense, no air). Now put a hissing s in front with no vowel: s-까이 → sky. One beat. Do the same for s-땁 → stop and s-꿀 → school.

In Korean, a final ㄱ, ㄷ, or ㅂ is held but not released (박, 밭, 밥). English final stops are also often held quietly, so this part is easy. The danger is adding 으 to release them: bed → 베드, robe → 로브. That adds a whole extra beat.
English uses another clue to tell bet and bed apart: the vowel before a voiced stop (b, d, g) is longer.
Two traps with final stops:

items: Adding 으: 베드, 로브, 백그 → each gains a beat. Keep the word to one beat (●). Close your mouth for the final sound and stop.
Merging: 백 for both back and bag. Let the vowel in bag take more time: ba—g.

blocks.html: 02 / Word groups
How to read the tables: Say Example A, then B, and then A again. Tap the beat pattern while you say each word.
A. Lips: /p/ vs /b/
B. Tongue tip: /t/ vs /d/
C. Back of tongue: /k/ vs /ɡ/

blocks.text: D. Puff vs. no puff after /s/
blocks.html: D. Puff vs. no puff after /s/
Spin still contains /p/, not /b/. Dictionaries write both words with /p/. The puff is the only difference, and English speakers do this automatically.

blocks.text: E. Final stops: one beat, and listen to the vowel length
blocks.html: E. Final stops: one beat, and listen to the vowel length
All of these words are one beat (●). In the right-hand column, stretch the vowel a little. Do not add 으.
F. Stops inside longer words

rows.html: PA-per · AP-ple · BA-by · RAB-bit · TICK-et · POCK-et · BAS-ket · COOK-ie · JACK-et · GAR-den · BIG-ger · DOL-lar
be-GIN · de-CIDE · to-DAY · a-GO · po-LICE · be-CAUSE

blocks.html: In words like potato, better, and ladder, the /t/ or /d/ between vowels often becomes a quick tap in American English. You will practice this in Lesson 06.

blocks.text: G. Stop + L or R clusters: no 으 in the middle
blocks.html: G. Stop + L or R clusters: no 으 in the middle
Korean splits these clusters with 으, adding a beat. Glue the two consonants together.

blocks.text: H. From words to short phrases
blocks.html: H. From words to short phrases
BUS stop: In a compound noun, the first word is usually strong: BUS stop, BOOK-store, CAR park, TEA-cup. You will learn more in Lesson 11.
03 / Rhythm drill: keep the 박자

blocks.text: Drill 1: Stretch the sentence, keep the claps
blocks.html: Drill 1: Stretch the sentence, keep the claps
Clap at a steady speed. The CAPITAL words land on the claps. Squeeze everything else in between.
Drill 2: The no-으 chain
Add one word at a time. The English column grows by one beat per line. Count how fast the Korean-style version grows.

rows.html: STOP at the BIG BLACK DESK
스톱 앳 더 빅 블랙 데스크

blocks.html: Check: Record the last line. If you hear a vowel after stop, big, black, or desk, say that word alone with your mouth closing on the final sound. Then put the line back together.

blocks.text: Short reading: Packing for the Boat Trip
blocks.html: Short reading: Packing for the Boat Trip
Goal: Use all four skills in one passage: /p b/, /t d/ vs /k ɡ/, the puff after /s/, and final stops without 으.
Focus: Read the passage once and mark the strong beats and pauses yourself. Then open the marked version to check, and read again while tapping.

Ben and Kate planned a short boat trip. Kate packed a picnic basket with peaches, cookies, and a big bottle of water. Ben checked the tickets and put a map in his pocket. At the gate, a guard asked them to wait. Their boat was still by the dock. While they waited, Kate spotted a small dog under a bench. The dog belonged to the guard, who gave it a quick pat. Soon, the gate opened, and their trip could begin.

blocks.summary: ▶ Marked version (open after your first reading)

blocks.html: BEN and KATE | PLANNED a SHORT BOAT TRIP. | KATE PACKED a PIC-nic BAS-ket | with PEACH-es, | COOK-ies, | and a BIG BOT-tle of WA-ter. | BEN CHECKED the TICK-ets | and PUT a MAP in his POCK-et. | At the GATE, | a GUARD ASKED them to WAIT. | Their BOAT was STILL by the DOCK. | While they WAIT-ed, | KATE SPOT-ted a SMALL DOG | un-der a BENCH. | The DOG be-LONGED to the GUARD, | who GAVE it a QUICK PAT. | SOON, | the GATE O-pened, | and their TRIP could be-GIN.

Reading focus: Find the two words that start with s + stop (still, spotted) and read them with the s+ㄸ / s+ㅃ trick. Then find four one-beat words that end in a stop (trip, boat, map, dock, dog, pat...). Read each one alone, then in its sentence.
05 / Check yourself

items: Which sounds use both lips: /p b/ or /t d/?
Does the missing puff in spin turn /p/ into /b/?
Stop ≈ s+땁. What Korean sound is sky close to?
Which vowel is longer: the one in bet or the one in bed?
How many beats are in bread, drive, and class? How many in 브레드?
What is wrong with saying bag as 배그?
No. It is still /p/. English speakers simply don't puff /p t k/ after /s/.
The vowel in bed. Vowels are longer before voiced final consonants.
It adds a second beat (으). Bag is one beat: a longer /æ/, then close on /ɡ/.

blocks.html: Before the next lesson, I can…

items: make a tissue move on pin and stay still on spin
say stop, sky, school in one beat each with the s+ㄸ/ㄲ trick
say bed, bag, robe in one beat with no 으, and with a longer vowel
say blue, bread, class, green without splitting the cluster

blocks.html: Before a voiced final consonant, the vowel is often longer than before its voiceless partner. This is a clue, not permission to drop the final consonant.
